accessibility.guidelines:
- The visible label merges into one native Button focus stop; the label and icons are not separate stops.
- Default, Hover, and Focus have the same accessibility semantics and are grouped as enabled.
- Disabled removes the control from keyboard focus order; expose its disabled state using the platform-native mechanism.
- Loading keeps one button stop and announces progress as a state; never expose the spinner as a separate control.
- Keep leading and trailing icons decorative because the API provides no separate accessible name for them.
- Keep the accessible name concise and action-focused; do not duplicate visible text with a second label.

states.description: Groups Figma Default, Hover, and Focus; these visual variants have the same screen reader semantics. The preview uses the Default variant.

states.description: Disabled button: zero focus stops; keep all three platform sections empty of focus-stop tables. VoiceOver (iOS): mark the control with the .notEnabled trait. TalkBack (Android): expose disabled() (or isEnabled=false for Views). ARIA (Web): prefer a native <button disabled>; for a custom button, expose aria-disabled="true" and suppress activation.
The loading indicator is decorative and remains part of the button; expose busy/loading through the button state without adding a focus stop.

api.generalNotes: Hover and focus are transient interaction states; the public API exposes persistent disabled and loading behavior as booleans. The Figma source models Disabled and Loading as mutually exclusive State variants and provides no combined case, so treat these props as mutually exclusive or define their combined behavior explicitly in application code.

summary.overview: Button is an action control with six visual variants and eight sizes. Its public behavior is expressed through disabled and loading props, with hover and focus handled as transient interaction states; optional built-in leading and trailing icons are independent. Structure is measured across every variant, size, and state, color treatments map to each visual variant, and assistive technology receives one button focus stop with disabled and busy semantics.
